x.ASV: A Psalm of David. Maschil. Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, Whose sin is covered.
x.Darby: Of David. Instruction. Blessed is he [whose] transgression is forgiven, [whose] sin is covered!
x.KJV: A Psalm of David, Maschil. Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered.
x.YLT: By David. --An Instruction. O the happiness of him whose transgression is forgiven, Whose sin is covered.

nt: The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a **maskil**. Since the meaning of this word is not certain, you may wish to represent it in its Hebrew form and spell it the way it sounds in your language. See the discussion of that term in the Introduction to Psalms.

David is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling, what constitutes true happiness from God’s perspective. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Oh, how happy is]

The expressions **transgression is lifted up** and **covered from sin** are passive verbal forms. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [the one whose transgression God has lifted up, the one whose sin God has covered]

These two phrases **the one whose transgression is lifted up** and **the one covered from sin** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and it would be good to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation rather than combining them. It may be helpful in your language to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [the one whose transgression is lifted up, that is, whose sin is covered]

Here the phrase **the one covered from sin** means “the one whose sin is covered.” David is speaking of sin as if it were an object that could be covered. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one whose sin Yahweh takes away]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **transgression** and **sin**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [the one forgiven of the wrong things that one has done, forgiven for how that one has disobeyed you]

Here, **one whose transgression is lifted up** and **one covered from sin** represent people in general, not specific individuals. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use expressions that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [anyone whose transgression is lifted up, and anyone who is covered from sin]

x.ASV: Blessed is the man unto whom Jehovah imputeth not iniquity, And in whose spirit there is no guile.
x.Darby: Blessed is the man unto whom Jehovah reckoneth not iniquity, and in whose spirit there is no guile!
x.KJV: Blessed is the man unto whom the Lord imputeth not iniquity, and in whose spirit there is no guile.
x.YLT: O the happiness of a man, To whom Jehovah imputeth not iniquity, And in whose spirit there is no deceit.

nt: David is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling, what constitutes true happiness from God’s perspective. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Oh, how happy is]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [any person]
לֹ֤א יַחְשֹׁ֬ב & עָוֺ֑ן וְ⁠אֵ֖ין בְּ⁠רוּח֣⁠וֹ רְמִיָּה

The abstract nouns **guilt** and **deceit** express the ideas of being guilty and being deceitful. If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **guilt** and **deceit**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [does not reckon what he has done wrong and who is not deceitful] or [does not reckon to him what he is guilty of and who does not act deceitfully]

Here, **spirit** represents the person’s inner being or character. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and in whom there is no]

x.ASV: When I kept silence, my bones wasted away Through my groaning all the day long.
x.Darby: When I kept silence, my bones waxed old, through my groaning all the day long.
x.KJV: When I kept silence, my bones waxed old through my roaring all the day long.
x.YLT: When I have kept silence, become old have my bones, Through my roaring all the day.

nt: By **kept silent**, David means that he did not confess his sin to God. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [When I kept silent about my sin]

Here David is speaking as if his **bones** were actually deteriorating. He means that his body was becoming weak, and he felt as if he was ill. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my vitality was depleted]

The word translated as **through** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [which caused me to scream]

David says **through my screaming** as an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [through my groaning]

David is using **all of the day** as a common expression of his culture to mean “continually.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [continually]

x.ASV: For day and night thy hand was heavy upon me: My moisture was changed as with the drought of summer. [Selah
x.Darby: For day and night thy hand was heavy upon me; my moisture was turned into the drought of summer. Selah.
x.KJV: For day and night thy hand was heavy upon me: my moisture is turned into the drought of summer. Selah.
x.YLT: When by day and by night Thy hand is heavy upon me, My moisture hath been changed Into the droughts of summer. Selah.

nt: The psalmist is referring to all of time by naming two major components, **day** and **night**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [continually] or [all of the time]

David is using **your hand was heavy upon me** as a common expression of his culture to mean that God afflicted or disciplined him severely. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly as in the UST.

The expression **My vitality was changed** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [God drained my strength] or [My strength dried up]

The point of this comparison is that just as the **heat of summer** is extremely intense and withering, so David’s **vitality was changed** due to his unconfessed sin. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [My strength was completely drained like something withered by intense heat]

nt: These two phrases **My sin I acknowledged to you** and **my guilt I did not cover** mean basically the same thing. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and it would be good to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation rather than combining them. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases with a word other than **and** in order to show that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [I confessed my sin to you—I did not hide my guilt]

Here David is speaking of **sin** and **guilt** as if they were something that could be covered. He means that he did not try to hide his sin from God. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and my guilt I did not refuse to confess]

See how you translated the similar expression in [32:1](../032/001.md). Alternate translation: [and you forgave the guilt of my sin] or [and you took away the guilt of my sin]

x.ASV: For this let every one that is godly pray unto thee in a time when thou mayest be found: Surely when the great waters overflow they shall not reach unto him.
x.Darby: For this shall every one that isgodly pray unto thee at a time when thou mayest be found: surely in the floods of great waters they will not reach him.
x.KJV: For this shall every one that is godly pray unto thee in a time when thou mayest be found: surely in the floods of great waters they shall not come nigh unto him.
x.YLT: For this doth every saintly one pray to Thee, As the time to find. Surely at an overflowing of many waters, Unto him they come not.

nt: Here David is speaking of God’s forgiveness as if it were something that could be found. He also indicates that there is a favorable time in which to seek forgiveness. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [while there is an opportunity]

Here David is speaking as if troubles were actually a **flood of great waters** that could overwhelm someone. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when great trouble comes, God will rescue those who trust in him]

Here, **him** represents godly people in general, not a specific person. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [to them]

x.ASV: Thou art my hiding-place; thou wilt preserve me from trouble; Thou wilt compass me about with songs of deliverance. [Selah
x.Darby: Thou art a hiding-place for me; thou preservest me from trouble; thou dost encompass me with songs of deliverance. Selah.
x.KJV: Thou art my hiding place; thou shalt preserve me from trouble; thou shalt compass me about with songs of deliverance. Selah.
x.YLT: Thou art a hiding-place for me, From distress Thou dost keep me, With songs of deliverance dost compass me. Selah.

nt: Here David is speaking as if Yahweh were actually a **hiding place**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You are the one who causes me to be safe] or [You are like a hiding place for me]

These two phrases **You are a hiding place for me** and **you preserve me from distress** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and it would be good to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation rather than combining them. Alternate translation: [You protect me as my refuge; you keep me safe from trouble]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **distress**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from things that cause me trouble] or [when others afflict me]

The implication is that there will be people around the writer who will be shouting joyfully about how God has rescued him. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [You surround me with people who are celebrating your deliverance with joyful shouts]

x.ASV: I will instruct thee and teach thee in the way which thou shalt go: I will counsel thee with mine eye upon thee.
x.Darby: I will instruct thee and teach thee the way in which thou shalt go; I will counsel [thee] with mine eye upon thee.
x.KJV: I will instruct thee and teach thee in the way which thou shalt go: I will guide thee with mine eye.
x.YLT: I cause thee to act wisely, And direct thee in the way that thou goest, I cause mine eye to take counsel concerning thee.

nt: The terms **instruct** and **teach** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [I will carefully teach you]

Here the psalmist is speaking of how a person lives as if that were a **way** or path that the person was walking along. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in how you should live] or [regarding how you should live]

Yahweh is using **with my eye upon you** as a common expression of the culture to mean “watching you closely and guiding you directly.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will teach you directly] or [I will look you in the eyes when I counsel you]

x.ASV: Be ye not as the horse, or as the mule, which have no understanding; Whose trappings must be bit and bridle to hold them in, Else they will not come near unto thee.
x.Darby: Be ye not as a horse, as a mule, which have no understanding: whose trappings must be bit and bridle, for restraint, or they will not come unto thee.
x.KJV: Be ye not as the horse, or as the mule, which have no understanding: whose mouth must be held in with bit and bridle, lest they come near unto thee.
x.YLT: Be ye not as a horse--as a mule, Without understanding, With bridle and bit, its ornaments, to curb, Not to come near unto thee.

nt: The point of this comparison is that just as a **horse** and a **mule** are stubborn animals that must be controlled with bits and bridles, so are people who refuse to follow God’s guidance. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Do not be stubborn like horses and mules that must be controlled with bits and bridles]

The psalmist assumes that his readers will know that here **ornament** refers to “trappings”, functional pieces that are used on horses and mules in order to guide and restrain them. The implication of the phrase **ornament of him to curb** is that a horse or mule must be controlled by these trappings in order to guide and restrain (or **curb**) them. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [his trappings must restrain him]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [ornament of him to curb his behavior]

A **bit and bridle** is a kind of harness that fits around a horse’s head and includes a metal bar that goes in its mouth. If your readers would not be familiar with what a bit and bridle are, you could use more general terms as in the UST or explain them in a footnote.

x.ASV: Many sorrows shall be to the wicked; But he that trusteth in Jehovah, lovingkindness shall compass him about.
x.Darby: Many sorrows hath the wicked; but he that confideth in Jehovah, loving-kindness shall encompass him.
x.KJV: Many sorrows shall be to the wicked: but he that trusteth in the Lord, mercy shall compass him about.
x.YLT: Many are the pains of the wicked; As to him who is trusting in Jehovah, Kindness doth compass him.

nt: The psalmist is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [Many are the pains of those who do wicked things]

The psalmist is speaking of **covenant faithfulness** as if it were a living thing that could protect someone by surrounding them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh’s faithful love will protect him] or [Yahweh’s covenant faithfulness will protect him]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [who acts faithfully toward him according to his covenant]

x.ASV: Be glad in Jehovah, and rejoice, ye righteous; And shout for joy, all ye that are upright in heart.
x.Darby: Rejoice in Jehovah, and be glad, ye righteous; and shout for joy, all ye upright in heart.
x.KJV: Be glad in the Lord, and rejoice, ye righteous: and shout for joy, all ye that are upright in heart.
x.YLT: Be glad in Jehovah, and rejoice, ye righteous, And sing, all ye upright of heart!

nt: See how you translated the phrase **the righteous** in [1:5](../001/005.md). Alternate translation: [righteous people] or [people who do what is right]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **joy**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and shout joyfully]

Here the **heart** represents where a person’s thoughts and motives exist. The phrase **upright of heart** describes people whose thoughts and motives are morally straight and righteous. Alternate translation: [all who think and act righteously] or [all who live with pure motives]
